intended_object: The canonical order isomorphism showing that a linearly ordered set α splits at a point x: α is the lexicographic (ordinal) sum of the initial segment {y < x} and the final segment {y ≥ x}. Inferred from the docstring and the name.
explanation:
The definition starts from the relation isomorphism `RelIso.sumLexComplLeft (· < ·) x`. That map identifies the lexicographic sum of {y | y < x} and {y | ¬ y < x} with α. It turns this into an order isomorphism with `ofRelIsoLT`. It then swaps {y | ¬ y < x} for `Ici x` using `orderIsoOfEq`, which is valid because in a linear order ¬ y < x is the same as x ≤ y. The result is exactly the ordinal-sum decomposition α ≅ Iio x ⊕ₗ Ici x.

The linear order hypothesis is needed. In a mere partial order, an element incomparable with x lies in neither Iio x nor Ici x, so the map could not be onto α. The generality is therefore natural.

This is Mathlib's own declaration. The companion `sumLexIicIoi` splits at x the other way round, putting x in the first piece; it is a different isomorphism, not another version of this one. So there is no separate counterpart to cite.
